notes: Rules are checked IN ORDER against the normalised (lower-case, accent-free) ingredient text. The first rule to match a piece of text claims it, so specific/safe rules must come before broad catch-alls (e.g. 'mineral oil' before 'oil'). 'pattern' is a JavaScript regular expression (case-insensitive). Optional 'eu' = EU/German regulatory or availability note. Levels: blue = helpful antifungal/anti-dandruff active, green = generally considered Malassezia-safe, amber = debated / depends on the person, red = known Malassezia food or trigger. See RESEARCH.md for sources.

rules.name: Ketoconazole
rules.why: Azole antifungal; first-line for seborrheic dermatitis and Malassezia folliculitis.
rules.eu: EU/DE: medicine, not a cosmetic. Terzolin® 2% Lösung (Apotheke, no prescription needed) — 2×/week, leave 3–5 min.

rules.name: Ciclopirox
rules.why: Broad-spectrum antifungal, effective on scalp SD.
rules.eu: EU/DE: medicine (shampoo/solution via pharmacy; ask a pharmacist or doctor).

rules.name: Zinc pyrithione
rules.why: Antifungal anti-dandruff active; lowers Malassezia and its irritating free fatty acids.
rules.eu: EU: BANNED in cosmetics since 1 March 2022 (CMR 1B, Reg. (EU) 2021/1902). You will only see it on non-EU or old stock.

rules.name: Selenium sulfide
rules.why: Antifungal anti-dandruff active.
rules.eu: EU: allowed in anti-dandruff shampoos up to 1% (e.g. Vichy Dercos Anti-Schuppen).

rules.name: Piroctone olamine
rules.why: Antifungal anti-dandruff active (Octopirox).
rules.eu: EU: the most common anti-dandruff active since the ZPT ban (Head & Shoulders EU, Balea, Sebamed, Isana).

rules.name: Climbazole
rules.why: Azole antifungal used in anti-dandruff shampoos.
rules.eu: EU: allowed up to 2% in rinse-off anti-dandruff shampoos (Reg. (EU) 2019/698).

rules.name: Salicylic acid
rules.why: Keratolytic: loosens scale so antifungals reach the scalp.

rules.name: Sulfur
rules.why: Antifungal and keratolytic.

rules.name: Coal tar
rules.why: Anti-proliferative anti-dandruff active.

rules.name: Undecylenic acid
rules.why: C11 fatty acid that is antifungal rather than a food.

rules.name: Tea tree oil
rules.why: Some antifungal evidence (5% shampoo trial), but can irritate or sensitise.

rules.name: Caprylic/capric triglyceride (MCT)
rules.why: C8–C10 chains are too short for Malassezia to use; widely listed as safe.

rules.name: C8–C10 acids/esters
rules.pattern: \b(caprylic acid|capric acid|glyceryl caprylate|glyceryl caprate|caprylyl glycol|propanediol dicaprylate)\b
rules.why: Short chains (≤C10) do not feed Malassezia; caprylic acid is mildly antifungal.

rules.name: Squalane
rules.why: Saturated hydrocarbon, not a fatty acid; listed as safe.

rules.name: Mineral oil / petrolatum
rules.why: Hydrocarbon, cannot be broken down into fatty acids by Malassezia.

rules.name: Synthetic hydrocarbons
rules.why: Hydrocarbon emollient, not a Malassezia food.

rules.name: Silicone
rules.why: Silicones are not lipids; not a Malassezia food.

rules.name: Glucoside surfactant
rules.why: Sugar-based surfactant; generally listed as safe.

rules.name: Sulfate / betaine surfactant
rules.why: Rinse-off surfactant; not considered a Malassezia food (can be drying/irritating).

rules.name: Coco-caprylate/caprate
rules.why: Mostly C8–C10, but the coconut alcohol part is longer-chain; lists disagree.

rules.name: Fatty alcohol
rules.why: Not esters; most fungal-acne lists say OK, but some people react. Watch if you flare.

rules.name: Ethoxylated fatty alcohol
rules.why: PEG-ether of a fatty alcohol; emulsifier. Lists disagree; some reports of flares.

rules.name: Emulsifying wax
rules.why: Blend of fatty alcohols and often polysorbate — check for polysorbate in the list.

rules.name: Ferment
rules.why: Yeast/bacterial ferments (e.g. Galactomyces) are commonly avoided by people with Malassezia folliculitis.

rules.name: Lecithin / phospholipid
rules.why: Malassezia secretes phospholipases and can harvest fatty acids from phospholipids.

rules.name: Wax
rules.pattern: \b(beeswax|cera alba|candelilla wax|euphorbia cerifera( \(candelilla\))? wax|carnauba wax|copernicia cerifera( \(carnauba\))? wax|rice bran wax|sunflower seed wax)\b
rules.why: Wax esters of long-chain acids/alcohols; less available than oils but lists disagree.

rules.name: Essential oil
rules.why: Essential oils are volatile terpenes, not fatty oils, but can irritate an already inflamed scalp.

rules.name: Algae / seaweed extract
rules.why: Flagged by several fungal-acne lists; evidence is weak.

rules.name: Ceramide
rules.why: Long-chain lipids; can contain fatty-acid residues. Low concentration usually.

rules.name: Polysorbate
rules.why: Polysorbate 40/80 is the lipid source in Dixon/Leeming-Notman agar used to grow Malassezia in the lab.

rules.name: Fatty acid (C12–C24)
rules.why: Free long-chain fatty acids are direct Malassezia food; oleic acid alone reproduces dandruff flaking.

rules.name: Fatty-acid ester / salt
rules.why: Esters (and soaps) of long-chain fatty acids are split by Malassezia lipases into food + irritating free fatty acids.

rules.name: Sorbitan ester
rules.why: Sorbitan + fatty-acid ester (Span); same family as polysorbates.

rules.name: Triglyceride / glyceride
rules.why: Triglycerides are exactly what Malassezia lipases break down for food.

rules.name: Cetyl esters / wax esters
rules.why: Long-chain wax esters; lipase substrate.

rules.name: Lanolin
rules.why: Wool-wax esters and fatty acids; a rich Malassezia lipid source.

rules.name: PEG fatty-acid ester
rules.why: Ethoxylated fatty-acid esters / castor oil derivatives; contain lipase-cleavable fatty acids.

rules.name: Plant oil / butter
rules.why: Plant oils and butters are mostly triglycerides of C16–C18 fatty acids (oleic, palmitic, stearic) — prime Malassezia food. Includes coconut, olive, argan, shea, castor, avocado, jojoba.
